chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

He said: He was asked about al-sukna (residence for life) and al-'umra (endowment for life), so he said: If he made the residence for his own life, it is as he stipulated. And if he made it for him and his descendants until their line ends, they cannot sell it nor bequeath it, then the house returns to its original owner.

Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man who houses another man in his house and for his descendants after him: He said: It is permissible, and they cannot sell it nor bequeath it. I asked: And a man who houses a man in his house for his life? He said: That is permissible. I asked: And a man who houses a man in his house without specifying a time? He said: It is permissible, and he can evict him whenever he wishes.

Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Husayn ibn Nu'aym from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who made a house a residence for a man for the days of his life, or made it for him and his descendants after him. Is it for him and his descendants as he stipulated? He said: Yes. I asked: If he needs it, does he sell it? He said: Yes. I asked: Does his sale invalidate the residence? He said: No, the sale does not invalidate the residence. Thus, I heard my father (peace be upon him) say: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: Sale does not invalidate rent nor residence, but he sells it on the condition that the buyer does not own what he bought until the residence expires as stipulated. And so with rent. I asked: If he returns to the tenant his money and all that was incumbent upon him regarding maintenance and construction for what he rented? He said: With good will and the tenant's satisfaction with that, there is no harm.

As for what al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Khalid ibn Nafi' al-Bajali from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who made a house a residence for a man for his life, meaning the owner of the house. Then the one for whom the residence was made died, and the one who was given the residence remained. Do you see that if the heirs wish to evict him from the house, they have that right? He said: I ask you, if the house is valued at a fair price, then one looks at one-third of the deceased's estate. If what is in his one-third covers the price of the house, the heirs cannot evict him. And if the one-third does not cover the price of the house, they can evict him. It was said to him: Do you see if the man for whom the residence was made died after the death of the owner of the house, does the residence belong to the heirs of the one for whom it was made? He said: No.

What was included in the beginning of this report from his saying 'meaning the owner of the house' is from the words of the narrator, and he erred in interpretation and made a mistake, because the rulings he mentioned afterwards are only valid if he made the residence for the duration of the life of the one he housed. At that time, it is valued and one looks at the consideration of one-third, its increase and decrease. And if the matter were as the interpreting narrator of the hadith mentioned, that he made it for the duration of the life of the owner of the house, then when he died, the residence would be voided, and there would be no need to value it and consider it with one-third. And we have clarified what indicates that.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Yusuf ibn Aqil from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding al-'umra that it is permissible for the one who endowed it. Whoever endows something as long as he lives, then it is for his heirs when he dies. This does not contradict what we presented, because his saying 'then it is for his heirs when he dies' means the one who made the 'umra, not the one for whom it was made. And if he meant the one for whom the 'umra was made, he would not have said 'it is for his heirs,' because when he dies, the 'umra returns to its owner if he is alive, and to his heirs if he is dead, unless it is made for him and his children and his descendants as long as one of them remains, as we clarified. And it is possible that what is meant by that is if he made the 'umra for another for the duration of his own life, then when the resident dies, it is for his heirs until he also dies, then it returns as inheritance according to what we said about it.

key_terms.الثُّلُث: One-third (of the estate, used in valuation for eviction)
key_terms.السُّكْنَى: Residence for life (a type of usufruct right)
key_terms.الْعُمْرَى: Endowment for life (a type of life estate)

ai.seo_question: What are the legal conditions for selling or evicting a tenant in a 'sukna' or 'umra' property arrangement in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith elucidates the jurisprudential distinctions between 'sukna' (life tenancy) and 'umra' (life endowment), emphasizing that these rights are personal and do not automatically transfer to heirs unless explicitly stipulated. It highlights the principle that a sale of the property does not invalidate the existing tenancy, ensuring stability for the resident, while also detailing the specific conditions under which heirs may reclaim the property based on the estate's value. The text further clarifies the interpretation of Imam al-Baqir's rulings regarding the 'one-third' rule for estate distribution when evicting a life tenant.
